parole.significato: A flat cargo vessel used on the Lower Rhine
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch aak.

From now-obsolete Dutch een afsteker maken (“to go by one of the boats of a ship”) (compare modern Dutch afsteken (“to set sail”)), synchronically analyzable as abstechen (“to cut out”) + -er; the German verb means in some contexts “to contrast, to diverge” and possibly also “to branch off” (compare

Borrowed from Dutch actie (“stock”), from Middle Dutch actie (“legal claim”), from Latin āctiō. Doublet of Aktion and Action. An earlier borrowing in the sense “legal claim” remained restricted to north-western Germany. In Dutch itself, both of the mentioned senses are obsolete.

Borrowed via Dutch ansjovis from Spanish anchovas, anchoas, plural of anchova, anchoa (“anchovy”), which is from Ligurian anciôa, through Vulgar Latin *apiuva from Latin aphyē, Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē, “small fry”).
Borrowed from Dutch abrikoos.

parole.significato: to watch out, to be alert
parole.testo: auf- + passen, a calque of Dutch oppassen. The sense “to be attentive” is not borrowed from French (as is the verb stem passen) but a native development of Dutch.
Loan translation and/or phonetic adaptation (17th c.) of Dutch oogmerk, from Middle Dutch ôghemerk. Analyzable as Auge + merken.
From baggern through interpretation of the syllable -er- as the suffix -er.
From Dutch baggeren, which pertains to bagger (“mud”). The noun Bagger (“excavator”) is a German derivative.
Borrowed from Dutch baai, which probably from French baie. Further origin uncertain.
From early modern Dutch bamboes (contemporary bamboe), from Portuguese bambus, plural of bambu, from Malay bambu, from Kannada ಬಂಬು (bambu).
From Dutch or English bark, both from Old French barque. Doublet of Barke.

parole.significato: baleen (plates in the mouth of the baleen whale)
parole.testo: Pertaining to Bart (“beard”). The form is most probably from the Dutch plural baarden, although contemporary Dutch uses balein.
Borrowed from Dutch batik, from Javanese bathik.
Borrowed from Dutch bezaan.

parole.significato: to condescend, to patronise, to treat as less than adult
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from Dutch betuttelen. By surface analysis, be- + tüdeln.
Short form of the marketing name “Schöner aus Boskoop”, after the Dutch town Boskoop where it was first cultivated.
Borrowed from Dutch brakwater, from Middle Dutch brak (“salty”). Compare brackig (which seems to be of Low German origin, although it could also be Dutch).

parole.significato: arsonist (person who has committed the act of arson)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Brand (“fire”) + stiften (“to bring about”) + -er (agentive suffix). The formation appears to be of Lower Rhenish origin, being first attested as Ripuarian brant stichter (1507) and Dutch brandtstichter (1542), both with the development ft > cht (as in Nichte etc.).
Borrowed from Dutch branding (also attested as Branding in German).
Borrowed from Dutch boegseren, from Portuguese puxar with influence of boeg (the cognate of German Bug (“bow of a ship”)), from Latin pulsare. Doublet of pulsieren.

Backformation of Dutch Boeren, plural of Boer. The word originally means “farmer” in Dutch but also in several German dialects, which is probably why the form Bur was avoided in German. (The word Bauer, and even more Bur as a dialectal form, may have the pejorative implication of an illiterate perso
From Busch + Mann, a calque of Dutch Bosjesman.
Borrowed from Dutch bui (which today usually refers to precipitation, not wind).
Borrowed from Dutch beurs, from Middle Dutch borse, from Old French borse (“purse”), from Late Latin bursa (“hide, purse”), from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa, “hide”).
From Dutch dek. Borrowed via German Low German Deck and hence with a plural in -s (Dutch uses dekken). The older Low German form is preserved in Verdeck. Cognate with English deck.

parole.significato: doit (small Dutch coin of minor value)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch duit, a historic coin of minor value. Cognate to Danish døjt.

parole.significato: A small size of type, standardized as 4 point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch diamant, used by Dirck Voskens who first cut it around 1700, presumably naming it by analogy with the larger Perl.

parole.significato: dock (a construction in which ships are repaired)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch or English dock, or via German Low German from Middle Low German docke. Possibly borrowed from Middle English dock; this form is attested a few decades earlier and the earliest Low German attestation refers to the harbours of London. The ultimate origin is uncertain; possibly fro
Calque of Dutch donderbus, Donner + Büchse, literally “thunder gun”.

parole.significato: Any of the sport leagues called eredivisie in the Netherlands and Belgium, especially that of association football.
parole.testo: From Ehre (“honour”) + Division (“division”), a calque of Dutch eredivisie.
From Eis (“ice”) + Berg (“mountain”), a calque of Dutch ijsberg.
From Elen (“elk”) + Antilope (“antelope”), after South African Dutch eland (literally “elk”).

From Erde (“earth”) + Ferkel (“piglet”), after South African Dutch aardvarken. First described in German by Peter Kolbe in 1719, who called it Erdschwein, a more literal calque. The form Erdferkel uses a word that is cognate with Dutch varken (“pig”) but has a slightly different sense.
From Feier or feiern + Biest, calque of Dutch feestbeest, itself probably a calque of English party animal. Coined in 2010 by Louis van Gaal, then coach of Bayern Munich.

parole.significato: small, hand-held telescope (including binoculars and monoculars)
parole.testo: Compound of fern (“far”) + Glas (“glass”), a loose calque of Dutch verrekijker.
Compound of fern (“far”) + Rohr (“tube”), a loose calque of Dutch verrekijker.
Borrowed from Dutch floers, a borrowing from French velours. Doublet of Velours.
First attested 1579. Borrowed from Dutch vrijbuiter (1572, but older). Analysable as frei (“free”) + Beute (“booty”) + -er.

Late 17th century, borrowed from Dutch frikadel (attested 1607), itself from French fricadel(le). The French is only recorded in 1742, but its earlier existence is likely as it is a variant of fricandeau (1548), which see. A further relation with Italian frittatella is speculative. Derivation of Ger
Unadapted borrowing from Dutch gabber. Doublet of Haberer and Chawer.

parole.significato: thin, translucid (often partly transparent) curtain covering a window
parole.testo: From early modern Dutch gardine (contemporary Dutch gordijn), from French courtine, from Old French cortine, from Late Latin cōrtīna (“curtain”).

parole.significato: reprehension, typically of the husband by his wife
parole.testo: Compound of Gardine (“curtain”) + Predigt (“sermon”). Probably a calque of Dutch gordijnpreek (an earlier form, now unused).
Borrowed from Dutch garnaal, earlier also garneel. Further origin unknown.

parole.significato: gas (matter in a physical state between liquid and plasma)
parole.testo: From Dutch gas. Doublet of Chaos.
Borrowed from Dutch gekko, further possibly from Malay [Term?] or Acehnese [Term?]. Compare English gecko for more.

Apparently not attested before the 17th century. Derived from ge- + fühlen; compare Gehör, Gesicht (both older). Perhaps a calque of Dutch gevoel. This is slightly earlier (16th c., doubtfully in 1450) and moreover Middle Dutch already made ample use of the nominalized infinitive gevoelen. Earlier H
Borrowed from Dutch geldbeurs. Equivalent to Geld (“money”) + Börse (“purse, wallet”).

From Dutch gieren, which is possibly the same word as that mentioned under etymology 1, with a semantic development “to scream, squeak” → “to make a repeated squeaking movement”. Alternatively from Dutch geren, also gieren (“to be askew”), from geer (“asymmetric piece of land”).

parole.significato: canal within a city (with residential buildings on either side)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch gracht, which pertains to the cognate of German graben (“to dig”).

parole.significato: touristic boat tour along the city canals (as operated in many Dutch cities)
parole.testo: Gracht + Rundfahrt. Probably a calque of Dutch grachtenrondvaart.

From Middle High German guldīn, gulden (“gold coin”, literally “golden”), from such forms as gulden pfenninc (“golden penny”), but especially from the gulden florīn (“golden florin”), a gold coin from Florence, which became popular in Germanic-speaking Europe since the late Middle Ages. Gulden was t

parole.significato: flag on the bow of a ship
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch geus or the diminutive geusje.
Borrowed from Dutch hagelslag.
Early 17th century, from Dutch haai, from Middle Dutch haey (15th c.), from Old Norse hár, há- (“shark”).
Borrowed from Dutch harpoen, which is usually considered a borrowing from French harpon (though this is contested).
Borrowed from Dutch harpoenier.
Borrowed from Dutch harpoeneren, from Dutch harpoen, possibly from French harpon.

parole.significato: Hottentot, a member of the Khoekhoe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch Hottentot.
17th century, from Dutch insolvent (1582). Equivalent to in- + solvent. The latter is younger in German.

From Dutch jacht (“yacht”), a reduction of jachtschip (literally “chase ship”). The spelling Yacht became standard in German under English influence, though it has now become less common again. For more, see English yacht (also borrowed from Dutch). Doublet of Jagd.

parole.significato: jeweler, jeweller (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: Probably from early modern Dutch juwelier, though the word is first attested in German. Analyzable as Juwel + -ier.

17th century, from Dutch kaai, from Middle Dutch kaey (whence also through hypercorrection Dutch kade). The word is ultimately Celtic, but it is unsettled whether the Dutch form is borrowed via Old French kay, as traditionally held, or indeed vice versa.
Borrowed from Dutch kaketoe, from Malay kakaktua.
Back-formation from the plural Kakerlaken of Kakerlak, which is the more original form of the word. The latter from Dutch kakkerlak.

parole.significato: to capture, to seize, to hijack (a ship or airplane)
parole.testo: Derived from Dutch kaper (“pirate”). The underlying Dutch verb is kapen.
Borrowed from Dutch katoen, ultimately from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun).
From kehren + Seite, borrowed from, or influenced by, Dutch keerzijde.
Borrowed from Dutch klinker, which pertains to the cognate of German klingen (“to sound”), from the clear sound the brick makes when struck against.
From Klippe + Dachs, calque of Dutch klipdas. First attested in the 19th century.

parole.significato: bag for food, especially while travelling; knapsack
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch knapzak (older form cnapsack), from Middle Dutch cnappen (“to bite with teeth”), ultimately from knappen (“to eat, crack”), of imitative origin, + Sack. Cognate with Low German knapzak. Compare German Schnappsack.

From Middle High German kriuzen (“to mark with a cross; crucify”), alteration (after the noun kriuze) of older krūzen, from Old High German krūzōn (“to crucify”). Equivalent to Kreuz + -en. The sense “cruise, patrol” (17th c.) is a semantic loan from Dutch kruisen, whence also English cruise.
Calque of Dutch kruiser, whence also English cruiser.
From early modern Dutch kust(e) (“coast”), from Old French coste (“side; coast”), from Latin costa (“rib”). Compare modern French côte, English coast.

From Dutch lakmoes, from Middle Dutch lecmoes, a compound of the cognates of German lecken (“to leak”) and Mus (“mush”). The former was later adapted to Dutch lak, German Lack (“varnish”). It seems obvious that there is a relation between Middle Dutch lecmoes and synonymous Old Norse litmosi (whence
Borrowed from Dutch leguaan. Ultimately from Taíno *iwana.

parole.significato: free of water, dry, empty (of a ship, especially its ballast tank)
parole.testo: 19th century, from Dutch lens (“slack, empty”, also “dry”, of a ship). Further origin uncertain.

parole.significato: to pump out or drain a ship
parole.testo: 19th century, derived from Dutch lens (“slack, empty”, also “dry”, of a ship).

16th century, borrowed along the Lower Rhine from Dutch loterye, lottrie (modern loterij), from Middle Dutch loterye (mid-15th c.), derived from lot, which is related with German Los. The Dutch word originated from the bilingual contact zones of Flanders and may be a Frenchified form of earlier Midd
From Dutch maalstroom; analyzable as mahlen (“to grind”) + Strom (“stream”). Compare English maelstrom.

Shortened from Matjeshering, which is borrowed from Dutch maatjesharing, from Middle Dutch medykenshering (literally “maiden herring”), formed from the cognates of German Mädchen (“girl”) and Hering (“herring”). The word was borrowed into several European languages, though the common term in contemp

parole.significato: seaman; sailor (of low rank) (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch matroos + -e, from Middle French matelots, from Old French matenot (“sailor, bunkmate”), most likely from Middle Dutch mattenoot (“bunk fellow”) or less likely Old Norse mǫtunautr (“food companion”).

Calque of Dutch meerderheid (1719), itself probably a calque (± 1600) of French pluralité (“majority”), originating 1559. Old High German mērheit (“quality of being more”) had no attested continuation. Analyzable as mehr (“more”) + -heit (“-hood”).

16th century, probably from Dutch muiterij, from Middle Dutch muiterie (attested 1350), eventually derived from Old French meute, whence also German Meute. The Middle Dutch itself might be from Middle French meuterie, which, however, is later and generally rare. While the Middle French is given by s

Borrowed from Dutch mops (“pug”). Further origin unsettled. Possibly a malicious use of mop (“German; Fritz; Kraut”), an early variant of mof. Alternatively from mopperen (“to grumble”), earlier also moppen, to which compare regional German möppern. The latter is plausible given the seemingly grumpy

parole.significato: muff (piece of fur or cloth, usually with open ends, used for keeping the hands warm)
parole.testo: From older Muffel, from Dutch muffel, from Old French moufle, Medieval Latin muffula.

parole.significato: blank, dud (lottery ticket that does not give a payout)
parole.testo: From early modern Dutch niet (“nothing”). Compare contemporary niets.

parole.significato: A small size of type, equivalent to 2 point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch non plus ultra, the name given to the type by the Enschedé Foundry in Haarlem, who first cut it. Doublet of Nonplusultra.
Borrowed from Dutch orkaan, from Spanish huracán, from Taíno *hurakā. Doublet of Hurrikan.

parole.significato: a unicellular ciliate protozoan of the Paramecium genus, first described by Antoni van Leeuwenhoek.
parole.testo: From Pantoffel + Tier + -chen. Likely a calque of Dutch pantoffeldiertje.
Borrowed from Dutch passaat via Low German.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or from; either
parole.testo: Early 17th century. Borrowed, perhaps through Dutch pinguïn (1595), from English penguin, which originally referred to the now extinct great auk. Further origin uncertain. Probably either from Welsh pen gwyn (literally “white head”), the great auk having two characteristic white patches near the eye
Borrowed from Dutch plakkaat, from Middle Dutch plakkaert, from French placard.

parole.significato: polder (land reclaimed from the sea by means of dikes)
parole.testo: Borrowed in the 18th century from Dutch polder, from Middle Dutch polre, from Old Dutch *polra (attested as polre in a Latin text). Further origin unknown.
From Pott + Asche, a calque of Dutch potas (older spelling potasch).
From Dutch pruim (piece of chewing tobacco).

parole.significato: quack, quacksalver (unqualified healer or incompetent doctor; male or unspecified sex)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Dutch kwakzalver, derived from Middle Dutch quacsalven (unsure whether verb or noun). Further origin disputed, though the second component is definitely Dutch zalf (“salve”).

parole.significato: border (ornamental bed, typically made from flowers)
parole.testo: From Dutch rabat from Middle French rabat ultimately a form of Old French rabatte. Cognate with German Rabatt

parole.significato: radish (Raphanus raphanistrum subsp. sativus, syn. Raphanus sativus)
parole.testo: Diminutive of earlier Radies, borrowed from Dutch radijs, itself from Middle French radice, from Italian radice, from Latin rādīx.
Borrowed from Dutch ransig

From Dutch ruiter (“robber; soldier; cavalryman”), from Middle Dutch ruter (“robber, looter”), from Old French routier, from rote, route, whence also German Rotte. The development from “robber” to “cavalryman” by association with Dutch rijder, ridder, German Reiter, Ritter. Later on, the word was co

parole.significato: rummer (kind of drinking glass, commonly used for wine in Germany; often made partially from coloured glass)
parole.testo: First attested in 1501 along the Lower Rhine. Possibly borrowed from Dutch roemer, also romer, although the Dutch is found slightly later (1524). The further origin is uncertain, but probably identical with etymology 1. At the time there seems to have been an interest in antique glasses unearthed in

16th century, at first in the more general sense of “stage, podium”, from Dutch schavot, from Middle Dutch scavot, scafaut, from Old French eschafaud, variant of chafaud, from Vulgar Latin *catafalicum, probably derived from Latin fala. Doublet of Katafalk.
A word of the Reformation, first attested ca. 1580, from Schein (“appearance, that which only seems to be”) + heilig (“holy”), likely after Dutch schijnheilig (1557).
Borrowed from Dutch schellak. Cognate with English shellac (“scale lac, lac thin like scales”).

parole.significato: destiny, fate (irresistible power that predetermines events)
parole.testo: 17th century, from schicken + -sal, after now archaic Dutch schiksel (16th c.).

parole.significato: to depict (with words), to narrate, tell vividly
parole.testo: 17th century, from Dutch schilderen (“to paint, picture”), in part through Middle Low German schildern. Equivalent to Schild (“shield”) + -er (agent suffix) + -n. From the painting of coats of arms on shields and related objects.

parole.significato: ready and capable to strike, attack
parole.testo: Mid-17th century, equivalent to Schlag (“hit, blow”) + fertig (“ready, capable”). Probably a calque of Dutch slagvaardig. For this speak the slightly earlier attestation (1625), the invariably nautical context of the earliest German attestations, and the fact that Dutch slag means “battle”. (The pro

parole.significato: chocolate (food made from ground roasted cocoa beans)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch chocolade, from Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.
Dutch schobbejak

parole.significato: rack, shelf, now mostly a large one in industrial or warehouse contexts
parole.testo: 16th century, from Dutch stellage. Equivalent to stellen + -age.
still + Leben, calque of Dutch stilleven.

First attested in the mid 17th century. Most likely borrowed from Early Modern Dutch stof, from Middle Dutch stoffe, borrowed from Old French estophe, estoffe, from estoffer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”). The word is ultimately Germanic and was borrowed into Old French from Old High

parole.significato: aida cloth, meshed cotton or linen fabric used for cross stitch embroidery or carpet weaving
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stramien, from Middle Dutch stramijn, stamijn, from Old French estamin, estamine (“light wool”), borrowed from Latin stāmineus (“full of threads, fibrous”), from stāmen (“thread”).

parole.significato: A slice of bread with a topping, which may include another slice of bread.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Dutch stul, or a variant of Stollen.

parole.significato: tea (drink made by infusing parts of a plant, especially leaves or buds of Camellia sinensis, in water)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Hokkien 茶 (tê), probably through Dutch thee. Attested since the 17th century.
From Trauer + Spiel. Attested 1630, hence possibly after Dutch treurspel (1584).
16th century, from Early Modern Dutch trense (now trens), from Spanish trenza.
Borrowed from Dutch tulp, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (dülbend), from Persian دلبند (dolband). Doublet of Tulipan.

Late 17th century, deverbal from verbinden, apparently after Dutch verband, from Middle Dutch verbant (ca. 1300), as several of the very earliest attestations are found in translations from Dutch (see citations page). Compare also Middle Low German vorbant (15th c.). By surface analysis, ver- + Band
From viele (“many”) + Ecke (“corner”), likely a calque of Dutch veelhoek, coined by Simon Stevin as a purism for Latin polygōnum, from Ancient Greek πολύγωνον (polúgōnon).

Mid-17th century, from Dutch waarschijnlijk (1540), itself a loan translation of French vraisemblable and/or Latin verisimilis (“probable”). Analysable as wahr (“true”) + scheinen (“to seem”) + -lich (“-ly”), thus “trueseemly, trueseeming”. Cognate to German Low German wohrschynlik.
Via Dutch walrus from an Old Norse source (cf. Danish hvalros). Secondary motivation in German as a compound of Wal (“whale”) + Ross (“horse”).
Late 17th century, from Dutch watten, from Middle French ouate, of unknown origin. Despite close semantics and phonetics, probably not from Proto-Germanic *wēdiz (“garment”).
17th century, borrowed from Dutch wouw, from Middle Dutch woude. Cognate with English weld, French gaude. Further origin unknown.

Wort (“word”) + Schatz (“treasure”). Cognate with Dutch woordenschat, Afrikaans woordeskat and Luxembourgish Wuertschatz. Attested since at least 1772 (see quote); possible calque of Dutch woordenschat.
17th century, from überbleiben (“to remain”) + -sel, likely after Dutch and Middle Dutch overblijfsel.
